props.title: Basic
props.initialSlug: Military thriller unravels deadly training mission

sections.content: Basic (2003) represents John McTiernan's late-career attempt to recapture the twisty military thriller magic of films like The Usual Suspects (1995) and A Few Good Men (1992). Set at a U.S. Army base in Panama, it follows John Travolta as an ex-Army Ranger turned DEA agent investigating the disappearance of elite Rangers during a training exercise. The film's complex narrative structure, with multiple unreliable narrators and conflicting accounts, draws from Rashomon (1950), though its execution lacks Kurosawa's masterful touch. McTiernan, who directed action classics like Die Hard (1988), struggles to balance the intricate plot with his trademark kinetic style.

sections.content: The military thriller genre peaked in the 1990s with films like Courage Under Fire (1996) and Rules of Engagement (2000). These films combined procedural elements with deeper examinations of military culture and morality. Basic attempts to follow this template while adding layers of conspiracy and deception. The film's rain-soaked Panama setting recalls Southern Comfort (1981) and creates a suitably oppressive atmosphere, but the constantly shifting perspectives and reveals ultimately become more confusing than compelling.

The pairing of John Travolta and Samuel L. Jackson, while meant to evoke their electric chemistry from Pulp Fiction (1994), falls flat here. Their scenes lack the Tarantino spark, instead getting buried under exposition and plot twists. The film's structure, with its multiple flashbacks and unreliable narrators, draws comparison to Memento (2000) and The Machinist (2004), but lacks their psychological depth and narrative precision. SUBHEAD: The Decline of the Military Thriller

sections.content: Basic marked a turning point for military thrillers, as the genre shifted away from complex narratives toward more straightforward action films like Behind Enemy Lines (2001) and Tears of the Sun (2003). The film's commercial and critical failure, along with similar reception for The General's Daughter (1999), suggested audiences were losing interest in labyrinthine military mysteries. Post-9/11, military films would focus more on contemporary warfare and real-world conflicts, as seen in Black Hawk Down (2001) and We Were Soldiers (2002).
